title: 1 Kings 19:1–18
context: After Carmel, Jezebel vows to take Elijah’s life, and he flees to Beersheba and then a day’s journey into the wilderness, where he sits under a juniper tree, often rendered broom tree, and asks to die. In verse 3 some manuscripts and ancient versions read that he was afraid, while the traditional Hebrew reading is that he saw; either is possible. An angel feeds him twice, and in the strength of that food he travels forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain, where wind, earthquake, and fire pass but the LORD is not in them, and then comes a still small voice, a Hebrew phrase variously understood as a gentle whisper, a quiet sound, or even a sound of near silence. The LORD answers Elijah’s complaint with new tasks, to anoint Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha, and with the word that he has reserved seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal, which Paul applies to a remnant according to the election of grace (Romans 11:4–5). Arminian and Reformed readers understand that remnant differently, as the notes at 19:18 explain, but most of the passage is shared ground about God’s tender care for a weary servant.

verses.text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ahab telling Jezebel all that Elijah had done, including killing the prophets. Victory is quickly followed by threat.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Ahab’s report as setting the stage for Jezebel’s fury. Readers in both traditions commonly note that Ahab does not respond to Carmel with repentance.

verses.text: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Jezebel swearing by the gods to take Elijah’s life by the next day. Her opposition is fierce and personal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see her vow as showing that even dramatic signs do not change a hardened heart. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sobering reminder of spiritual opposition.

verses.text: When he saw that, he arose and ran for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah running for his life to Beersheba and leaving his servant there. The bold prophet now flees.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his flight as showing the frailty of even great servants (compare James 5:17). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with compassion rather than condemnation.

verses.text: But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah going into the wilderness, sitting under a juniper tree, and asking to die. His despair is deep and honest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his prayer as echoing others who asked God to take their lives (compare Numbers 11:15; Jonah 4:3). Both traditions commonly read the verse with pastoral care for those who feel overwhelmed.

verses.text: He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah lying down to sleep and an angel touching him and telling him to eat. God meets him gently in his exhaustion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the angel as God’s ministering servant (compare Hebrews 1:14). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as God caring for the body before addressing the heart.

verses.text: He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a cake and a jar of water beside Elijah, and him eating and drinking before lying down again. Simple provision restores him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s tender care for his exhausted servant (compare Psalm 103:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a reminder that rest and food matter in spiritual struggle.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s angel coming again, telling Elijah to eat because the journey is too great for him. God knows his limits.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated care as patient grace for a weary prophet. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as comfort for those who feel their strength is gone (compare Isaiah 40:29).

verses.text: He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah traveling forty days and forty nights in the strength of that food to Horeb, God’s Mountain. God sustains him for the journey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see echoes of Moses at the mountain (compare Exodus 24:18). Both traditions commonly read the verse as God leading Elijah to a place of renewed encounter.

verses.text: He came to a cave there, and camped there; and behold, the LORD’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah lodging in a cave and the LORD asking what he is doing there. God’s question invites honest reflection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as gentle confrontation from the LORD who already knows. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as God drawing out his servant’s heart.

verses.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah pouring out his zeal for the LORD and his sense that he alone is left. His complaint is honest but partly mistaken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his words, later cited by Paul (Romans 11:3), as showing how isolation can distort perspective. Both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy for his discouragement.

verses.text: He said, “Go out and stand on the mountain before the LORD.” Behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Elijah to stand on the mountain as a great wind, earthquake, and fire pass, but the LORD is not in them. God is not confined to dramatic displays.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see echoes of the LORD passing by Moses on the mountain (compare Exodus 33:22). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as preparing for a quieter revelation.

verses.text: After the earthquake a fire passed; but the LORD was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the still small voice following the fire as God’s gentle way of meeting Elijah. They commonly see in it God’s patient, personal approach to a discouraged servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the still small voice as God’s quiet word, though they commonly avoid making it a rule for how God always speaks. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact meaning of the phrase with care.

verses.text: When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah wrapping his face in his mantle and standing at the cave entrance when he hears the voice. Reverence marks his response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covering of his face as awe before God’s presence. Both traditions commonly note that the same question is repeated, inviting Elijah to reconsider.

verses.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for the LORD, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Elijah repeating his complaint word for word. His perspective has not yet changed despite the encounter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as showing that God’s revelation will now be followed by a corrective word. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with patience toward a weary servant.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, “Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD sending Elijah back on his way to anoint Hazael king over Syria. God answers despair with new work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over the nations, even Syria (compare 2 Kings 8:13). Both traditions commonly read the verse as restoring Elijah’s sense of purpose.

verses.text: Anoint Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel; and anoint Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel Meholah to be prophet in your place.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see God commanding Elijah to anoint Jehu as king over Israel and Elisha as prophet in his place. Elijah is not alone, and his work will continue.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God providing successors for his purposes (compare 2 Kings 9:6). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as comfort that God’s work does not depend on one person.

verses.text: He who escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and he who escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD describing how those who escape Hazael will fall to Jehu, and those who escape Jehu to Elisha. Judgment on Baal worship will be thorough.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s plan for judgment unfolding through human agents. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, recognizing it as covenant judgment within Israel’s history.

verses.text: Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth that has not kissed him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the seven thousand who have not bowed to Baal as faithful believers whom God preserves, and they commonly read Paul’s use of the verse in Romans 11:4–5 as a remnant chosen in Christ, with faith as the condition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in I reserved God’s own sovereign preservation of a faithful remnant, and they commonly read Romans 11:5 as an election of grace that precedes and produces faith. Both traditions commonly agree that the remnant exists by God’s grace and not by human merit.
